title: Lesson 6: Integration Patterns: Request-Reply, Fire-and-Forget, and Batch (Inbound & Outbound)
description: The three archetype integration patterns every Salesforce architect must recognize (request-reply, fire-and-forget, and batch data synchronization), plus the selection matrix, the limits that shape each choice, and a worked example that combines all three.

questions.question: When should an integration use the request-reply pattern?
options: When the caller must wait and act on the response immediately.
When the caller hands off the work and never waits for any result.
When large volumes move on a nightly schedule.
When data must be replicated in bulk in either direction.
questions.explanation: Request-reply is synchronous: the caller blocks for the response and updates its state from it, which only works for small, real-time interactions.

questions.question: Why does a fire-and-forget integration usually need a callback?
options: Because the event bus guarantees delivery to every subscriber.
Because platform events can be rolled back just like ordinary database transactions.
Because the remote system processes later and its key is not known yet.
Because the caller must block until the remote process has finished.
questions.explanation: Because the handoff is asynchronous, the remote system reports its created key back through a callback rather than returning it in the original call.

questions.question: What makes a batch data synchronization a good fit?
options: A single record that must be confirmed while a user waits.
A large volume where timeliness matters less than throughput and safety.
A payment that must be authorized and displayed before the page returns.
A change that must reach a warehouse within one second.
questions.explanation: Batch moves large volumes on a schedule, so it is chosen when throughput and safe, re-runnable loads matter more than immediate updates.
